utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. You were continuing where you left off yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I'd pretty nearly concluded what I need to say. I'd explained how both these witnesses required either full protection or confidentiality until the moment they came to court, how we -- the orders had been obtained reflecting their concerns and positions to obtain protection until court, how in the case of General Vasiljevic we had at one stage asked for closed-session testimony and that had been declined, so that in the run-up to the trial they still had the benefit of pseudonyms and delayed disclosure for the reasons stated, how it was clear that there came a time when General Vasiljevic was going to be prepared to give evidence in open session but that he wanted protection until he got here for reasons of security risks which were all too real, and how in any event, not least because of the developing experience of threats to witnesses associated with this trial, it's necessary to be cautious about abandoning protection until the witnesses are quite sure that's what they want to do. In our motion of the 31st of May of 2002, paragraph 15, we said this, that these witnesses will also require certain protective measures relating to their testimony before the Trial Chamber. This was sensitive source witnesses generally. The Prosecution will be in a better position to assess the extent of the protective measures required in relation to those particular witnesses closer to the time at which they will testify, enabling the minimum necessary protective measures to be applied. The Prosecution therefore requests that it be permitted to file an application for the trial-related protective for sensitive source witnesses at a time closer to the date of their testimony. And the Prosecution submits that it will be appropriate to file such applications on the same date that the sensitive source witnesses's statements are to be disclosed to the amici, that is, 30 days before the witness is expected to testify. Well, that position didn't reflect the possibility of there being no requirement at that time for protective measures at trial, and it may be that counsel of perfection would have had us, at the 30-day period for a witness who was not going to require protection, to serve a notice upon the accused and Chamber at that stage. And that's clearly what we should do for the future for any witnesses who have protection of the kind identified by the Rule and for whom it is known 30 days before trial that no court protection will be required. A couple of matters of detail. I said that I would tell you a little more about this witness and his requirements for confidentiality. It will be interesting to see what he says about this if he's asked about it by anyone in evidence, but the reason that he was given cash or money to buy his own airline tickets is because right up and until the moment that he came to court, he did not wish to be associated with the OTP, and of course if VWU pays for travel, as it does in most cases, then the local airline, the local Yugoslav airline, knows and is able to communicate to others that the travel has been paid for by this office. And it was specifically to avoid that risk and as a mark of his requirement for confidentiality that the witness required to be given the money in order to buy his own airline ticket and pay for his own accommodation so little did he want to be associated with us in any public way. You will remember that following the disclosure of his name to the associates 24 hours later, he claimed to have received a threat, and his coming to give evidence was the subject of press reporting, which concerned us and the Chamber. Before he left, he then gave a press conference to say he was coming, entirely out of the blue and unknown to us in advance. These are all matters that may be explored with him. But as it was understood by us, right up and until the moment when he stepped on the aeroplane, he was somebody who wanted his dealings with us dealt with on a basis of strict and practical confidentiality. One other point about one of these witnesses, C-039, General Vasiljevic, the accused's complaint about inability to prepare hardly applies in the case of this witness when his material was disclosed in full to the accused on the 3rd of July of last year. Before I sit down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go back to one matter which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Having heard your explanation about these two witnesses, what I think the Chamber will be concerned with is to ensure that, as far as possible, this kind of miscommunication or misunderstanding is avoided in the future. And you -- what you're suggesting is that the Prosecution in future would file an application on 30-days notice. I'm not sure if I follow what you propose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me make it clear. My error. It had been -- had been our intention and has been our practice where seeking protective measures at court for sensitive source witnesses, to file an application 30 days ahead of hearing or usually longer, i.e., at the same time that we provide the material to the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you would -- you would -- what you propose is to file your notice at least 30 days --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- in advance, at which stage you would be contacting the witness to see what the position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. And if at that stage we knew that no application had to be made, then although no application has to be made, we should then communicate by filing a notice in court or by other informal means that are properly recorded, we should be notifying the parties that our understanding is that the witness will give evidence publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The amici suggested you get an affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's unrealistic in real terms. These witnesses may be still elsewhere, and it simply won't be possible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you shouldn't get a signed, if not an affidavit, some signed declaration from them that they want this protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When they come to Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not when they come to court, 30 days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean sending an investigator on a special mission to some part of the world? It could be America. It could be Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Send a letter. Why not send a letter with an enclosed document saying, "If you want protection, sign this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The advantage of that, it seems to me, Mr. Nice, is that it is then clear that the decision is activated by their request, by their desire. Sometimes when the OTP makes a decision on its own, it is clear now that it is done in circumstances that are ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, with respect, there may be ambiguity in the way it's presented at the moment, but as Your Honour said yesterday, seeking protection proprio motu is both envisaged by the Rules, and nobody suggests that's other than proper, and of course, for sensitive source witnesses, something that is almost inevitably proper to apply for in the particular and potentially dangerous circumstances of this trial. As to getting signed documents from witnesses 30 days before, if I may say so, it sounds comparatively easy in theory. I suspect it will prove to be extremely difficult in practice, and I would respectfully suggest that providing we make our position clear one way or another 30 days before, or more, so that nobody's left in any ambiguity, this would be preferable really for the following reason: What often happens is that witnesses come here with protection - or not often, frequently happens - and we are able to satisfy or have been able to satisfy them that it's better to give evidence in open session, which is the way the Court prefers. Occasionally it's gone the other way and they've come open and sought protection. Getting them, by writing 30 days before, to express an opinion is likely to lead to a solidification of views that it might be better was, frankly, more flexible and more responsive to the immediate circumstances in which they find themselves. And there will be, in reality, no conceivable prejudice if it's known 30 days before, by communication with the witness, that the witness seeks pseudonym, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just add a couple of things? I'm reminded, of course, that a further problem is that witnesses frequently have a false and an excessive view of what may be available to them by way of protection and general assistance. They may hold that view despite having been perfectly, properly spoken to by investigators when they make statements. They develop false ideas of what's available and on offer. Well, nothing's on offer, but what's potentially available. If we write to them or fax them, whoever has faxes and whatever else, we may find ourselves in the troublesome position of having statements from them that have to be corrected or reinterpreted and so on. It's very difficult. It's far better and accords with our experience, if I may respectfully say so, to establish at least 30 days before a witness comes whether he or she will want protection, and at that stage then the explanation must be given with sufficient clarity that the witness will only be seeking through us a level of protection that is one that may be afforded by the Court and which one which we are prepared to support. At the same time, if we forecast that the witness will be giving evidence without protection, we can tell the Court and the accused and the amici that. If when the witness comes to court and when the final position is established, as it can only be established really by face-to-face discussions for many witnesses, any changes will be communicated immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mentioned 30 days it seems to me because you have a notion that 30 days would be a sufficient period for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Because for protected witnesses, those for whom delayed disclosure has been granted, the Court's order is that 30 days is the time when documents go to the amici. So that given that the danger justifies delayed disclosure, or the risks justify delayed disclosure until for one of the involved participants 30 days, then it should be 30 days or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Really, the issue is if this procedure is set afoot, which way should we, the Court, and the Prosecution, be satisfied that everything possible has been done to avoid situations in which there is protection but at the very last minute it's removed? I understand, of course, some witnesses are persuaded, it may be, to remove protection, which of course is in the interests of justice, but it's really the sensitive witnesses on the delayed disclosure that is the crucial element.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. See --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be you could tell us how many more you have in mind to call. I don't expect an answer now, of course, but it can be worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Several. Probably a dozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this case, nothing was done that was either wrong or improper or contrary to the Rules. The only thing that happened was that as opposed -- where we weren't making a positive application at the 30-day period for protective measures at Court, it didn't occur to us that at that stage we should have said to the parties in fact this witness will give evidence openly although he will remain fully protected from public scrutiny until the date of his arrival, because both General Vasiljevic and this witness, subject to what he says, required secrecy or confidentiality until they got here. There is no other explanation for the present witness's insistence on masking his cooperation with us by having cash for his ticket. So that's what we'd ask you to approve of, and we would adjust our practices to ensure that not only parties know at the earliest opportunity, maybe earlier than 30 days but that at least 30 days we indicate one way or another there's going to be an application for protection or not at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Another alternative would be a statement from the investigator who spoke to the witness to say -- to describe the conversation which he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The 30-day period notification could come in that form, and of course, if it was an application for protection, you'd have to have that affidavit or that document from the investigator in any event in support of the application. Your Honours, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At least in that way we -- everybody would know what the attitude of the witness was to protection at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that would clear up that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought -- we've got a witness, and the sooner we get on with it, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just two other points then. C-039 was disclosed in July in B/C/S and September in English last year. And just while you're seized of this particular problem, there's a new category of a sort of difficulty, but I'll just tell you what it is. There are two witnesses coming up, C-031 and C-032. C-031's approach is that he will be prepared to go public, but he's only going to make that decision if and when he gets a satisfactory waiver of liability for revealing state secrets from the government. So this is a new sort of complicating factor. C-032 has now apparently indicated firmly that he doesn't seek protection at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just see about C-032. He doesn't seek protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At trial, and likewise C-035. C-035 will not seek protection at trial, either. C-031 won't seek protection provided he gets a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But dealing with -- dealing with 32 and 35, then, for the moment, there will be no protective measures sought then. But they're not subject to the delayed disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think -- I'll check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you. Could you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It's already disclosed, a long time ago, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff tells me, and her knowledge is usually encyclopedic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have to be careful about C-031. If he would only make up his mind when he gets the waiver, then we could end up in the same situation where at the very last minute he decides to go public and the accused would not have had -- would only have had ten days to do his investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff shaking her head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, further details of that, I'm grateful to

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: C-031 has already been disclosed in any event. The only question is whether he's going to go public. So far as we know, the waiver has been already granted, he hasn't yet received it. Once he receives it, there will be no further problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know how long the Court wants to spend on this at this stage, but there are some observations that we have that relate to the whole disclosure issue as well, because it can be seen by the Court that it's a very great burden to get through this material for big witnesses in such a short period of time for an accused. We have disclosure of their statements and the dates have been given by the Prosecutor, but we have the supporting material, but we have no idea that General Vasiljevic is going to refer to these particular documents at all amongst the 300.000 or so served. So to get a picture of his evidence and how it's actually going to unfold in court doesn't really materialise until you get the summary. Likewise with Captain Dragan. Of course we get his statement and we don't know what's going to be produced through him, what particular document that's been found in Brcko or elsewhere to prove a particular point, if he can recognise it. And likewise with the 10.000 pages on the CD-ROMs. So we're all having to work under very great pressure here to try and get an idea of what the evidence is going to be. There's a basic disclosure, but understanding what the nature of the case is going to be through the witness is an entirely different matter, and that's something that we would like to make clear, which is a factor which is added to when one is dealing with late disclosure as a result of anonymity. It is a great burden on the Defence side of the court. There are threats and threats as well. There's a threat like to the English cricket team in Zimbabwe, which is hardly earth shattering, and one does wonder whether some of this is at a scale of heightened hysteria that is simply inappropriate. I know the Tribunal has a duty under the Statute, and the Rules indeed, to pay regard to victims, and protective measures, but one can't help thinking, associated with this case and other cases, that everything is taken at far greater height of hysteria than is really necessary. Sometimes when these matters are investigated, they come to absolutely nothing. I don't know how far the Court wants to go into the matter at this stage, but it may be that this whole issue of disclosure to the accused would certainly be worth a half an hour of the Court's time at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We probably need to reflect on it, and we need to make sure that there is, for the rest of the Prosecution case, a system that is fair to all. I'm not sure I agree with what you say about protection. It has proved in this Tribunal to be a real problem, and we've had in this case evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some of these witnesses with protective measures, I am told - I'm not an expert on the history and politics and all associated matters - is it's blindingly obvious who they are. When they give their evidence, everyone can work out who a person is from the perspective of their evidence. And sometimes fault is laid, I am told, at the Defence door. Allegations are made by the Prosecution that it can only be the Defence, and I am told by those who observe this trial that it's blindingly obvious to some journalists who a particular witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem has been not necessarily the revelation of who the witness is but, of course, another totally unrelated -- not totally unrelated problem but another problem is the disclosure of statements - that's been the problem - which are protected. But we will need to think about this, I think. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, and we will revert to it. Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly do. What you said at the end is very true, that the issue of disclosure of documents is an essential issue that has to do with time. We heard a moment ago Mr. Nice citing the example of Vasiljevic, saying that his statement was disclosed in July. So in his words, it was no problem to review it. But I suppose it is easy to make a distinction between possibilities concerning a secret witness and a public witness. In the case of a secret witness, only my two associates know who it is and can gather facts. When we are talking about a public witness, I can engage a larger number of people for gathering information. So my manoeuvring space for gathering information is essentially different, depending on whether a witness is treated as a secret one or a public one. That is one thing I wanted to say, a very substantial one. Secondly, Mr. Nice is putting things upside down. He's making us believe that it should be the rule that all witnesses should be secret and then announcing, just before testifying, that they no longer want to be secret. This witness should be an exception to the rule, and I understand it was your intention too. I can't understand why one should be worrying more about the witness being a greater Catholic than the Pope if the witness himself is not asking for protective measures. Why should they be invented and insisted on by the opposite side if the witness doesn't want them? I can only understand it as obstruction of my future cross-examination not of protection of the witness. In the first contact of the witness with the Prosecution, he can state clearly whether he needs protective measures and whether he wants to be a secret or a public witness. Why should this be a mystery that is revealed only 30 days before the witnesses testify? It turned out here that none of the witnesses who spoke in secret proceedings of some sort was in any danger except in verbal explanations given here. If this is an exception indeed, then you should treat it as an exception, and it should be clarified in due time. This is not the first time that a witness is proclaimed to be a public one only when he appears in the courtroom whereas he was treated as secret during the entire period of preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm developing an interpretation of Rule 69, which I think obviously has to be construed in the light of the provision in the Statute which says that trials are to be public, which in any event is a very basic and customary Rule. And in order to make that Rule consistent with that requirement, it seems reasonable to me that it must be construed that the right which it gives the Prosecution to apply for protective measures should only be exercised on the basis of a clear request from the particular witness concerned. Otherwise, we come very close to a position that is just identified by Mr. Milosevic, which is that there is a routinisation in the application for protective measures in respect of witnesses whom the Prosecution sees as being sensitive when in fact it has to be an exception to the position stated in the Statute. So I would want to urge the position that that Rule must be construed in a manner that makes it consistent with the basic requirement under the Statute for public trials, and that what it means then is that the Prosecutor should only apply for the protective measures on the basis of a clear and explicit request from the particular witness for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see this is a developing interpretation, and I think that to reply now without further consideration, especially in terms of -- in light of the precise terms of the Rule, might have rather serious institutional consequences. But there are also practical problems or practical consequences. I think - I may be wrong and I need to discuss this more with some of the investigators - but I rather suspect that to make too much of a point of saying to witnesses it's now or never, yes or no, and they'll all ask for protection. And an objective assessment of risk is actually very important, because -- an objective assessment along with the views of the witnesses themselves. Mr. Kay's point is, quite respectfully, completely wrong. It's a very dangerous place out there for these people. Those of us who visit the territory know that. Those of us who read summaries of what's in the local press know that. It's a very dangerous place. An objective assessment linked to expressed desires at an early stage is probably going to keep to a minimum the number of applications that are made for delayed disclosure and will certainly keep to a minimum the number applications made at trial. Put in the vernacular, the last thing we seek to do for witnesses whom we judge it unlikely to be appropriate is to encourage them to think about protective measures, because by and large, if you do that, people will say, yes, please. Not all, but some or many. So I can understand how, superficially, it's attractive to think that we could reinterpret the Rule in the way Your Honour proposes, but I think it would have or may have serious practical consequences and certainly would have institutional consequences and I think I can say we would like a little more -- should that be advanced in any way a final decision, we'd like a little more time to bring to you the experience of our investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't expressing a final decision. It's a developing construction that I have, and it is a matter that we'll have to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's always helpful to have Your Honour's views on these matters, and we'll bear them in mind and I'll find out a little bit more what our inspector -- investigators can advise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll return to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I missed that, Mr. Milosevic. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a very specific question to what Mr. Robinson just said. I understood him as saying that protective measures may be introduced if the witness is asking for them. A moment ago, Mr. Nice said that C-032 and C-035 are not asking for protective measures. Why are they on the list of protected witnesses at all if they're not asking for them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have taken the matter as far as we can today. No doubt we can return to it when these particular witnesses come to give evidence. But let us now have the witness back and continue with the evidence which we have to do today and allow him to get away. Let me deal with one thing while -- the witness is here. Just one matter so everyone has notice of it. Dr. Ranta has been contacted and would be available to give evidence on the 12th of March, and we have in mind to call her then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will mark our calendars appropriately. I can't remember whether there's anybody who's absolutely committed to that date. I'll come back to you if there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you let us know just as soon as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll be calling that witness on the 12th of March. So you've got notice of it. We will have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry you've been kept waiting. We had some other matters to deal with. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, before I continue with my questions relating to the substance of your testimony, I would like us to discuss something first. We had started cross-examination with my question as to whether you had asked for protective measures, whether you had asked to be a protected witness. Do you remember that? That was yesterday. Your answer was that you had asked for no protective measures, no protection, and you never expressed the desire to testify in secret at any time before you came to testify here. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember, I suppose - just tell me yes or no - that Judge May asked Mr. Nice to explain, because I was right. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, regarding that explanation, I want to ask you a question. Mr. Nice is claiming that you had asked that all your contacts with that so-called Prosecution be entirely confidential. My question now is: Did you ask that your contacts with this so-called Prosecution be entirely confidential?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation will have to be a little longer; I can't say just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been cooperating with The Hague Tribunal for a number of months, since the Agreement on Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal has been adopted, since the law has been adopted. Since I am a public figure, to protect me from journalists and from the need to give explanations, I didn't want my contacts with the Prosecution to be discussed in public. But at no point in time -- we even discussed this, Mr. Milosevic, when they asked me whether I wanted to be protected. I told them it was nonsense, because it was obvious from the text that it can only be me. From all I said, it's clear that it can be no one else. So at no point in time could I have imagined that you or your side had been deprived of the information that I would be testifying in this court. But to be quite frank, I believe that it was their assessment and they provided this protection to protect me from problems I might have in my own country, from journalists, et cetera. So it is not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste any more time. I understand your explanation. A moment ago, Mr. Nice said that you were also the subject of certain threats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But those threats would not have been the reason for you to ask to testify in secret?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly not. I reported these threats to our competent authorities in Yugoslavia. That has nothing to do with you. This issue has been verified, and it has been established that these threats can have nothing to do with you and could in no way endanger you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've cleared that up now. Very well. I have before me a special report of European observers dated 29 March 1994, which reports a conversation with you. I will quote only a portion of your statements and ask you to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It talks about you, and it says: "Personally, he favoured -- [In English] but in reality, the most important thing was to stop the war." [Interpretation] So was it the prevailing climate that everybody wanted to stop the war as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the feeling that you expressed too? Because you were then in Krajina. You were appointed there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Especially the people who waged the war felt like that, because they know best all the horrors of war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The sentence was: "Personally he favoured an independent Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please comment on this as well: [In English] "Catholic, Muslim, and German lobby was very strong and greatly influenced the world's opinion on Serbs. Also because of geography, those journalists who did come to cover Krajina came to Zagreb where they were unduly influenced by a very smooth Croatian PR effort." [Interpretation] What did you know about this entire media war, the demonisation of Serbs, and the efforts to represent them as the bad guys in the circumstances in Krajina where they were fighting for their lives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that anyone who even superficially followed the media war - and as we know, the media war is a very important aspect of the war in general - it was clear that on the one hand there was the German lobby, there was a Catholic lobby, there was the Muslim lobby, and on the other hand there was the Orthodox lobby which was, as we all know, because of the dubious support of Russia due to your policy, but that is your problem. But I felt through my personal experience that if a journalist comes to Belgrade and comes to see me first, I don't waste time making a friend out of him, and throughout the war, that journalist would report in favour of the Serbs. Since most journalists arrived through Zagreb -- and I have to say that Croats had a much better attitude - I know this from my own sources - Croats invested a lot of effort and money in receiving these journalists, whereas our side felt the journalists were enemies and received them accordingly. So it is our own fault that we lost this media war. But let me confirm what you are saying. There were many, many lies, and as we all know, in war the first victim is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please comment on this. It says: "Captain Dragan stated that this current war [In English] stated that this current war was an extension of World War II in which Germany was still battling Serbs through Croatia." [Interpretation] Do you mean that even the present borders in the territory of the former Yugoslavia are very much like those established by Hitler and Mussolini in World War II?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My ex-wife is German, so I felt on my own skin the changes in German attitude towards me, because they realised I was not an Australian, I was a Serb, because until then, they thought I was an Australian. After German unification, it is my own conviction that I'm speaking of now based my feelings rather than information, that Croatia is again turning into the Independent State of Croatia that existed in the times of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the circles in which you moved among Serbs, it was a feeling that was not only a matter of emotion, it was something they felt on their own skins?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that you are proud, but let me quote: "[Previous translation continues] [In English] ... that during his operations in Croatian territory, not one Croatian civilian had been killed or injured. Captain Dragan felt that the presence of his soldiers in the area saved many Croat lives." [Interpretation] Can it be inferred on the basis of this that this defence over there was only defence, true defence, resorting to the right to self-defence? It's not that crimes were committed. At least where the organised forces of defence could keep matters under their control to the best of their ability.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. But if you give a me a minute, perhaps it would be useful for the Tribunal if I would paint a picture for you what the feeling at the front line is like which you in these warm and clean offices will never feel. No matter how well educated you are and what age you are, all of you here, you will never be able to imagine the fear in the eyes of unarmed civilians, prisoners, women and children, when an armed soldier with a rifle walks up to them. When that soldier abuses all his supremacy over such persons, that is certainly a great sin. I experienced that. I was that enemy soldier who had that rifle in his hands, and believe me, I tried at every moment to select targets where -- that were military targets only, and I severely punished even the thought that soldiers might have to strike at anyone else. And that is what the Tribunal knew about me even before I came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Captain. Generally speaking now with regard to this particular question of the Red Berets, I asked you yesterday about this, that these were the Red Berets of Krajina. They mentioned the Red Berets of Brcko, Teslic, Skelani, et cetera. All of that was linked up to some secret service of Serbia, whatever, but we clarified that. There's a report here that corroborates this also in general terms. [In English] "Vosaka [phoen] Training Camp. Training camp of Captain Dragan, 22 September 1993." [Interpretation] Again, this is in the materials that I got from the other side, and it says here concerning your courses, that is: "[In English] The camp appeared well maintained but very spartan. The courses taught at the camp include a 21-day basic level military skills course for," [interpretation] 14 days, et cetera, et cetera, and then, finally, this is what I want to read: [In English] "On completion of the specialist course, graduates are given the red beret and the qualification badge." [Interpretation] So persons who were enrolled in your courses, persons who were involved in the defence of Krajina, when they would complete a course, then they would get a red beret.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it says here, as regards your own feelings, that there are many undisciplined persons - "mob" is the word that you used - with very little leadership at lower levels and at medium level and that that is the reason why there is so much violence and so many acts of destruction on both sides. Is that the assessment that can be made regarding what was going on on both sides?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the report, which is again a special report -- 7 September 1993 is its date, and it refers to discussions with you. These are teams, Sibenik, Gospic, Split, centre Zadar, visit to the Krajina. It says: "There are many armed civilians in Krajina." And then they say: "From the political and military discussion they had with you, after having said that there were many armed civilians, amateurs, as you had put it, [In English] "the European Community led by Germany is responsible for the current situation as a result of recognition of Croatia and embargo put against Serbia." [Interpretation] Do you know that many European and world politicians believe that the premature recognition of Croatia, which was first carried out by Germany -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now getting far from the witness's evidence. It's not for the witness to talk about the world politicians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this happens to coincide with what he's been saying, so I wanted to -- it to be obvious what the impression was in Krajina, because nobody believed this. Nobody thought that administrative borders could be recognised and that the right of a people who had their constitutional status according to the constitution would be denied altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what people felt in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one brief question. We're going to move on to the other ones as well. Do you know that there were trials in Krajina that had to do with crimes committed against Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me about the details, because really, I was so busy with my very own line of work that I was really not interested in police work and court proceedings. But I was informed, though, that there were proceedings. I know that some people were arrested. And I, as a matter of fact, participated in the arrest of individuals who had violated some codes of military conduct. So there were proceedings. I'm convinced of that. I heard discussions to that effect too, but please don't ask me about the names or the dates, because there are other people who can speak about this far more competently here than I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude, since you were not sent by the service or invited by the service, that the only representative of the service who spoke to you privately before you left was Franko Simatovic? It's not only that he did not encourage you to go. According to your very own testimony, he said to you, "You are trying to kill yourself." Is that the way he put?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Those were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said then, "If I were afraid of that, I wouldn't go in the first place." But at any rate, is it clear, because this was an informal conversation, it's not only that the service was not sending you but this one man you knew was trying to talk you out of going there precisely by using those words, "You're trying to kill yourself."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And ultimately, this contributed to my return. Certainly they were not pushing me to go there against somebody's will or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he himself said to you, according to your testimony here, although his tasks were exclusively devoted to intelligence, he said that everything was secret and that if his bosses knew that he was going there, that he would be arrested or dismissed from the service altogether.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mentioned several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to clarify another matter which has to do with suggestions that you received. You mentioned Filipovic and Radonjic, namely that you should leave Yugoslavia and so on and so forth. Did they threaten you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now, after so many years and after having known Frenki for several years, perhaps I could give a better explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This came all of a sudden, beyond anybody's expectations, beyond my own expectations. There was so much fuss around me, and I clashed with Seselj, and I started giving statements that would have sounded different in a peaceful country like Australia, for example, but in that country, perhaps they were a bit unrestrained. I had the feeling that somebody in the service passed a decision to the effect that I was a potential problem, and they tried to resolve the question of me, and they thought that I would get frightened and that I'd pack up and leave. However, they made a mistake. They apologised. Jovica apologised himself, and he said, "Let's bury the hatchet," and we did bury the hatchet. But for about two years the relationship was very cool. We had no contacts whatsoever. But then slowly things started getting into the right place. I'm not sure, I'm not convinced that it was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you don't think that it could have come from a higher place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that this came from the very top. But people do that often. I mean, it's quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you quite openly. You don't even have to answer this at all if you don't think this way. Don't even give me an allusion by way of an answer. In Krajina, did you come across the following: That various politicians were invoking my name and hiding behind my name when they tried to win political points for their own benefit? Did you come across things like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Tribunal is going to find this very hard to understand, because this is so characteristic of our very own people, because this is the characteristic of our own people. Because you know, if somebody in Australia was to tell me, "I'm Mr. Howard's man," you know what I would think about that? But do you know what happened to me in Belgrade? I saw people being arrested in Belgrade because they said that they were captains, men that they had to do with the fund, et cetera. And in Krajina, as far as you're concerned, I think that one out of every three people said that he was your best friend, that he was your best man or whatever, or Senta's friend, and so on and so forth. So I had a lot of experience in this field. And if they had photographs taken with you, then this was taken to be major proof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's quite clear that there were so many manipulations. You know about that both in Serbia and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to use this not for the purposes for which you said this, but I would like to challenge what a previous witness said, the previous witness. You explained that a journalist advised you to go and see Nedeljko Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That could have been only in the second half of 1992, because it is only then that he became chief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was he then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vasiljevic was in office until May, I think, as far as I can remember. I'm sure that we have it in the transcript. Now, when Vasiljevic left office, then Boskovic came in. But let's leave that aside. Vasiljevic has claimed something that I wish to question, but let me ask another question before that. Nedeljko Boskovic advised you to record everything so that he could use that against the service.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's just put it the other way: In order to protect me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this had to do with relations with the state security service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Vasiljevic claimed here that Nedeljko Boskovic was appointed to this particular position in the army by the State Security Service of Serbia. This is an incredible claim, but that's the way he put it. And that Nedeljko Boskovic came to head the service because he was sent there by the State Security Service of Serbia. Is that your impression? Did you have the feeling that it was the State Security Service of Serbia that stood behind Nedeljko Boskovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about this, I give you my word. But after 12 years of socialising with the high official from the state security service and having known Jovica Stanisic, because we were friends after that, there was this fantastic animosity between the service and Boskovic and the service and the army. I don't think that there could have been anything. I mean, I'm really convinced of this. I don't know. This was open animosity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But as regards your concrete relationship with him and the proposals he made to you, could anyone draw the conclusion that he was a man of the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believe that the opposite is true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never record this material and have it until the present day. It is illogical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were asked here about the documents of the Captain Dragan Fund, and you said that it has over 60.000 proteges or, rather, persons it had helped, and there are files on each and every one of these persons. You were asked about a few persons, but there are over 60.000 of them, so I assume that there are reasons for each and every one of them, verified reasons. Now, is it always the case that somebody was a victim of the war and that someone was a casualty in conflict or was a family member of such a person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You went too far. It is sufficient for any person to have been a war victim, period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were shown some papers that were signed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, and it says there how a particular person was wounded, where, et cetera, that these were members of the Serb volunteer guard. And then the question was put to you whether social welfare had to do with these volunteers as well. And now I'm asking you, why would this not pertain to volunteers? Can you find any reason why this social welfare would not pertain to volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it. War victim, period, irrespective of ethnicity, irrespective of the units where they served. We even have cases of Muslims and Croats who received assistance. Very few because I did not have much information about that, but it wasn't sure who they were wounded by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course, you know that already at the beginning of the war in Bosnia or, rather, in Serbia we had over 70.000 Muslim refugees in Serbia from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that they were treated equally to others, with full equality, and that they were protected, that nobody discriminated against them in any way and that nobody attacked them in any way? I do not know of a single case of this kind. Do you know of any cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I know about cases when these people were helped, these people who were in trouble. There were at least two Muslims that I got out of some prisons, although I had nothing to do with Bosnia. And I had never heard of these persons before that. And I did not get anything for that or did I ask for anything for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The representative for the other side asked you, because he showed you here the law on basic rules pertaining to military invalids, this Yugoslav law about the basic rights of military invalids, did it pertain to Arkan's men? That was the question that was put to you. And I'm asking you now why would it not pertain to those persons who had become military invalids? Do you see any reason why it should not pertain to then as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't. They too are war victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the Red Berets, since it seems that during the examination-in-chief the person you were most asked about was a man called Zika, Crnogorac, I wish to ask you something about him. You were shown a file from the Captain Dragan Fund where he signed a receipt, a certificate, saying that a certain Jovan Vejnovic joined your camp and your unit in Knin, and this was popularly referred to as the Knindza unit. And I have seen here that on the 8th of August, he joined. Later on, he was wounded. Tell me something about this Zika, Crnogorac. You said that he was your favourite cadet because he was the first one you arrested.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since there's a certificate saying that on the 8th of August, 1992, he joined, he had to have been a commander of your Knindzas in the Krajina at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, yes. But there's something -- could I -- could I please have a copy of the certificate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have a copy. It was shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only saw it on the monitor. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's tab 4 of 391, if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's on the monitor once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I get a hard copy, please? Thank you. [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Everything is clear to me now. This is a certificate saying that this man --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says on the 8th of August, 1992, he joined the unit in Knin, the Knindza.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA was already holding this, and the Knindza formally disappeared on the day I left the Krajina. I was not in Knin at that time, but in order to explain to someone in the fund that these people were from Knin, they were all referred to as the Knindza. I didn't care about that. It wasn't important to me. What was important to me was that it should be evident from this that he was really -- that he had really been wounded, that he was not simply pretending.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wasn't it the JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it couldn't have been the JNA at that time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then it was the Serbian army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since my question relates to Zika --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zika, Crnogorac. Where was in 1992? Was he in the Krajina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow their movements really, but Zika left the Krajina soon after I did, and he went to Fruska Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the brief period when some 15 of your men were on Fruska Gora, and after that, they went back individually?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all went their own way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of this special operations unit of the state security service, and if so, from what time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you this because I really didn't keep tabs on individuals who were all over the place. Zika did go over. Maybe he was even employed for a while, because some of these young men from the Krajina were employed. But I really don't have this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, your information is from the time he was in the Serbian army of the Krajina regardless of where he moved.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you where Zika, Crnogorac, was on the 27th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speakers pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You hear that request, both of you. Pause, please, between question and answer. The interpreters need to be able to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to ask you about the connections between your unit and this unit for special operations of the Serbian state security service. Is it true that one might say that the only connection between your Knindza and the special operations unit was that several of your fighters, after you left the Krajina, went with you, and then later on some of them were received into the special operations unit of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more than ten men and certainly less than 20, and not all at the same time but in twos and threes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At various time periods and during the special procedure all proceed into that unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and some of them are still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I get various newspapers from Serbia here, and recently I saw in a magazine a photograph, and it was actually an announcement, an advertisement for recruits. This was very well done. It's the best unit the police has. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it might be very useful for the Tribunal, because this unit has been mentioned very often and will continue to be mentioned during these proceedings: I professionally, with some ten others monitors, observed this unit over a ten-day period, and there is a document -- over a 21-day period, and there is a document which should be read in order to dispel the erroneous image that this unit has created in the minds of people. I have a lot of things in my head, but it would take me only five minutes to explain about this unit. It might be useful for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it might be useful if you explain, because the worst crimes have been ascribed to this unit with no foundation, and I want to dispel these false ideas here. So please explain.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Soon after your visit, I and ten other highly-educated people from the service and from the police were asked to put together a team that would observe this unit in a very intensive exercise. This unit was of the size of an independent company. It never reached the level of a battalion. This was absolutely the best unit that we have in the armed forces of Yugoslavia, without any doubt. But according to some international standards, this is far below the level of an ordinary infantry unit in Iraq today, for example. If I had to choose, if I were to have at my disposal this unit, this company, or a squad of -- an ordinary Australian infantry squad, I would have to choose the latter, because although by far the best in the country, it's far below the level expected of a company in a modern army, equipped with modern weapons and with the support that such a unit would have in any other country. What you saw, Mr. Milosevic, that's all. There is nothing else, because when the president arrived, they took out everything, everything that was in good order, everything that was not in good order. Even the cooks put on uniforms in order to make the unit look more impressive. And this is quite understandable. There is a 50-page report, and if you read it in order -- we wanted to show all the weaknesses and the failings of that unit, with the best of intentions, of course. This unit was at the level of a company, but its efficiency was that -- was equivalent to the efficiency of a squad in a Western army, and this was very little for a state, for a country at war, such as Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of this unit committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I know a lot of these men. I've read a lot of bad things about them. But I've already read a lot of bad things about myself, about Frenki, and so on. All these men know me. I may know not each and every one of them, but they all know me, and they know what my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standpoint was, the standpoint of the Knindza. Traditionally, they feel that they are the successors of the Knindza. If there were any individual cases of crimes, I would love this to be revealed and these people to be tried so that the Knindza can once again be the pride of our nation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This unit is said to have committed a crime in Teslic where they cut up the stomachs of some 20 people, ripped them open. And it is even well-known who committed this crime and that this unit has nothing to do with it. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. I know nothing about it. And I apologise if I'm breaking the rules, but I do wish to say something of importance for the Tribunal and for you. I can explain in great detail what the system of defence of the Krajina was, and I think the same system was used in other war theatres later on, and this will explain how things functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first part of the war, the entire theatre was under the control of police stations. Each police station had its area of responsibility, and later on they were joined by the Territorial Defence which then shared this responsibility. All this was put under the single command of the JNA when it was left without any Serbs, Croats, and so on, when only Serbs were left in it and when the JNA joined the war. When the JNA joined the war, the entire war theatre was divided into areas of responsibility. Each area of responsibility had its own commander. And to illustrate how important this is, I'll give you an example that everyone in the Krajina knows about. Martic's deputy, the second most important man for the defence of the Krajina, once came to my area of responsibility, and he dropped a cigarette butt onto the floor, onto the ground, and I forced him to pick it up because this was my area of responsibility, and I felt totally responsible for everything that was happening in my area of responsibility. So that wherever a crime happened, there is someone in whose area of responsibility this happened, and there is documentation to show this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I think. This will be easy to establish. So please tell me now, when you were training these men and when with ten other experts you observed an exercise and evaluated it, you were not a member of the state security of the republic of Serbia, and you were never its member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I never had an identity paper of the state security service, and I never ever received any remuneration from them apart from these 2.200 dinars that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now comment on the film that we saw. There is no doubt that there was a review of this unit and that I was present at a celebration in May 1997.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 4th or 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know because I was on vacation in Karadjordjevo nearby and I went to visit them on the occasion of that celebration. So let's comment on a few things now. Do you know that this unit was established only in 1995 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I wasn't interested in that. I should know because I have a lot of friends there, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But there is no doubt that this unit was established after the war and that this unit wanted, among other things, to use the symbol of the Red Berets in order to carry on the tradition of the Knindzas. And you yourself said that in that unit, later on, there were perhaps only some ten or a dozen men who were previously in your unit, in the armed units of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is. I don't think there were any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in order not to be too generous towards you and what you were doing, it is my impression that this unit wanted, in a way, to affirm the tradition of other courageous fighters who throughout the Krajina and the Republika Srpska fought in the defence from the key words or, rather, according to the key words in Frenki Simatovic's speech.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that Frenki started the drive to collect as many war souvenirs as possible so that we could set up a museum, and you saw this. And as concerns the establishment of the unit, of course since Frenki was engaged in intelligence work on the ground, he was always surrounded by a group of people, and at certain moments Zika was probably part of that group, or at least I assume he was. And I just want to explain this document which says the MUP of the Krajina. I don't know what kind of stamp this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here the MUP of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are coming to a conclusion, so if you would just -- Mr. Vasiljkovic, if you would just finish what you were saying and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Frenki wanted to put all this together with a single goal. He said that armed forces have to have a tradition, and he appropriated this, and he felt that this was a very serious piece of work, and he did it well. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in order to ascribe alleged crimes to this unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us take the adjournment now. We can come back to this matter in 20 minutes. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Captain, it is not disputed that it was the wish of this unit to promote the tradition of the struggle for the defence of the Serb people in the territory of Krajina, of Republika Srpska, or anywhere elsewhere where they were defending themselves, regardless of the fact that this unit did not participate in each of these battles for defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. We introduced some confusion with these documents before this Tribunal. If it doesn't matter, it doesn't matter, but it is my impression that there is some confusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of confusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that we might have created the impression -- a wrong impression regarding this Zika, Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wanted precisely to establish that when he was issuing these certificates he couldn't have been elsewhere. He was in -- a member of the Serbian police in the army of the Serbian Krajina. He was not a member of the service.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not of Frenki's age, and I never looked at his papers, his ID, but I don't see what's wrong with it. He's one of the men who could have been both a member of the Serbian service at some other time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the keyword, at some other time, in some later period.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could have only been after you left. It could not have been at the same time when you were in Krajina. It could have been only later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've cleared this up now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did we? So while he was with you, he was not a member of that unit. He could only have joined the unit later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back again to that video footage. I'm not asking it to be played again, but in that speech made by Franko Simatovic at the time, those critical words he uttered, I'll remind you, were: "The struggle against war crimes, genocide, and terror," is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what he was trying to promote, struggle against war crimes, genocide, and terror.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we all believed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of the people who participated in that struggle against war crimes, genocide, and terror should be proud. I still believe they should be proud of themselves for fighting genocide, war crimes, and terror. Was that so, Captain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, since it is indisputable, even from that footage where we see that it is not a unit large enough to make up even an infantry company --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that it was never larger than at the time when you attended that celebration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the unit was set up in 1995 or 1996, but it doesn't matter. We'll establish that on the basis of other documents. Do you remember from that footage that a group of officers was introduced to me, and they were referred to as veterans, and I shook hands with them, you remember. They were lined up in front of me. Do you remember that from the film?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perfect. Did you notice that about ten of them - I wasn't really counting, I saw this film here for the first time, and it reminded me - that about ten of them were colonels; right? Then there were several majors, and so on and so forth. So the highest ranking officers under the rank of general; is that correct? Is it clear, then, since the unit was never larger than an infantry company, that they could not have been members of that unit in the sense of a combat detachment? Those were people from all areas who could have been there later as advisors, instructors, in other positions, because what would ten colonels be doing in one company? Is my assumption correct? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's good that you remarked on this. We have to be realistic. A good part of these colonels were semi-literate. In this way, Frenki was trying to pay his respect to these young men who have, in one way or another, been useful to the service. Only those men who received that knife, which you received too and so did I, not even all of them received it. One part of them are the original men who came from Krajina in that period. Don't forget that I received from the alliance of special units of the Greek army a similar decoration. The opposite side saw this. This certainly doesn't mean an engagement or affiliation. It was a form of recognition, praise, a token that somebody thought of them. Certainly such a number of colonels could not technically be within the composition of one company. It was done symbolically. It was even offered to me, and I refused. I said you would be demoting me, in a way. It was just a token of respect. It was for the president that we made this show and put together such a number of colonels. It was a nice theatrical show, using people of the highest rank, the largest number we could possibly find.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But tell me this, since Simatkovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Simatovic. In his speech, he refers to these veterans. Is it clear then that these veterans were subsequent potential members of that unit who fought in various places in the Republic of Serbian Krajina or Republika Srpska but not within that unit? They could have fought as members of various units of the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was ever in dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, so I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it must be perfectly clear that the unit we are talking about, the unit we saw on that film, as such was never or could never have been in all those locations in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It is rather the case that its members later fought elsewhere in various battles after being members of the army of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a typical example is Benkovac. I never heard of a battle for Benkovac. Everybody knows what happened in Krajina. With all those reports of the UNPROFOR, have you ever heard any such thing? I talked to those people and I received some intelligence from them. It's not good to name them because they're still serving. But nothing could have happened there without any of us seeing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but one thing is clear: You were present at that celebration.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not in the capacity as a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was an honourary guest, just as you were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also saw on that film that the president of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia was there too.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and so were secretaries, assistants, porters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were also many civilian figures. It was a celebration where you were just a guest, and you remarked quite correctly I was a guest too, and many other people appeared there as guests, invited to the celebration. They were not there as members of that unit, regardless of whether they were wearing uniforms or not. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must even tell you that I received a uniform that I didn't want to wear that day. So that many other people wore uniforms just because they were given them to look better, and even some people who received those knives were not members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we can agree that it is absolutely clear, absolutely correct that there is no continuity between your unit and that unit. We are talking only about a small number of members of your unit which were later received into your unit, into the JSO, and participated in various battles.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember well that in that speech where he praised the members, he also mentioned the establishment of the Captain Dragan Fund.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I know, you established that fund.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the unit certainly has nothing to do with it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
