utterances.text: 28th of 8th, 1991 -- 2001. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's a year and some months before the law on cooperation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I honestly didn't consider this, what we talked, that that was the -- that that was the -- that was just what I remembered, quickly; a lot of suggestions, a lot of suggested things that I didn't think was important, and I said yes. Like I said, I was called by Stanisic. I just didn't think was important to go into all those details, signed that I told Frenki to go and visit Stanisic, and gave me the number. It was enough to say that I was called by Stanisic and that would be correct. But if you want to grab like that -- so I don't think anything is a lie here, but were they Grey Wolves or Wolves, or were they -- you know, you can get me on that: "Did you say Grey Wolves?" Might have, because I didn't think that the "grey" was important. Important that they're Wolves. So I think that this is a very inaccurate statement, and I think would be fair, if you wanted to question me on this statement, then you have started from -- when we had the time, to go right through it and clarify that. I think we cleaned this statement, by your investigator, we corrected all those things that I felt was maybe incorrect. Like Vasiljevic, for example. I was sure that that was Vasiljevic. I believed that was Vasiljevic. I even put it. I made another mistake but that was just because I believed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, the Chamber has both statements now and I'm sure will review them carefully.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I just feel I been tricked in that and you been dishonest about it, I'm sorry. And I very regret that this is how it ended. I don't think that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us before that you were a personal friend of Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very personal friend, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you seem him just prior to coming up to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to see him 15 minutes before I arrived over here. I thought you should do that with a friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you discuss with him the fact that you were coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After arriving here, have you had any communication whatsoever, either by phone or e-mail or any form of communication with Mr. Simatovic or anybody connected with the Serbian state security service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called Simatovic on his private phone just to say hello, that I'm okay, and we did not -- and I just told him, How did you like what you heard? And he says, Well, you just said what had happened. And I said, Yes, but it wasn't very easy to come here and say all this. That's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did you spend discussing your testimony with Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all about 20 seconds. And after that was -- after that was a discussion such as we're going to have dinner when we come back, and we're going to -- like I said, he's my friend for 12 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you spoke with Frenki Simatovic while you were in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once that I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yesterday. Last night, or afternoon, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning, when you said as part of your testimony that you had discussed the film with Frenki Simatovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not discuss the film. I'm sorry, sir. I mean this morning, yesterday, fifteen seconds just to tell him I'm alive, I'm here. You know, are you watching? And that's it. There was no discussion on any parts of whatever is, and he says I think you just said how it was. And you probably recording my conversation and it would be nice to show it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody was recording your conversation, sir. You have testified that you did not see the film until you arrived here, and you testified earlier today --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said that I've seen some parts of that film, but I've seen it in this form only here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please make pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, I have no further questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to deal with the two exhibits, in fact, which we haven't. There was the Nin magazine article. There was then a statement and the statement of the witness of the 10th of February this year. So -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar will deal with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should the Nin article in fact go in? Because nothing materialised from it through this witness, as the Court will recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We allow articles in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Nin article will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 393. And the statement dated the 10th to the 17th February will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 392.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we part from the most recent discussion and just by way of reminding you of something and putting something in context, you'll probably recall that well before Rade Markovic gave evidence, I was forecasting that we would be calling witnesses whom we would only be advancing in part for the truth of their evidence. And that you will recall, in Markovic's case, we produced evidence, called evidence to prove the truth of a statement that he had made and from which he departed in evidence. We, of course, take a witness statement from the investigator who took the last witness's statement and we'll consider applying for leave to call him. There is another witness available. He's actually come over especially from England for today. He won't be finished today, and he's obviously got to come back. There are also some administrative matters that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will be dealing with, although I think they may be taken more shortly because there's been a written filing to assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to start the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to start him. He's a witness who's 92 -- semi-bis'd, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see how we get on with the administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or alternatively, we could do the administrative material now so that we know exactly how far we've got with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more convenient to deal with the statements now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with them, if that's what you're suggesting. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've got your latest filing. B-1732, I don't know if we need keep these numbers, whether we can't refer to him by his name. Any reason why we need to keep the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the moment, you want to reconsider the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we actually -- we will file something later similar to what we had filed for General Mangan and Mr. Davies, something at a later stage when some evidence of Bosnia has been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. So we won't pursue that one. We've had -- we've had an additional witness, Edgar Rousseau. It may be convenient, if we can, to deal with him next week too. And indeed perhaps you would have a look to see if there are any other Vukovar witnesses or witnesses from that area who it might be convenient to deal with together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Your Honours, we intended to file in -- a motion related to witnesses we would like to tender in the mode of 92 bis (D), and these are actually the witnesses who had testified in the Dokmanovic case, and we hadn't done that so far because we actually had expected you to make a decision on a similar filing from the Bosnia section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not -- I can tell you we're not ruling on Bosnia for the moment. We're going to stay with Croatia. But I was going to raise with you, anyway, that question about the Dokmanovic witnesses being dealt with perhaps in the same way as Dr. Bosanac. One of them gives fairly important evidence, I would have thought. But in any event, could you file that as soon as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there are any other Vukovar witnesses who it might be convenient to deal with at the same time as we -- those that I've mentioned, perhaps you could let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will file that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take them location by location. Now, that leaves us -- we'll deal with Rousseau next week, and that leaves us with the two, 1201 and 1231, and there really is a simple issue here, that they made their statements -- they made their statements. 1201, the events -- he was aged 11 the events he described. He made his statement nine years later. 1231, he was aged 9, and he made his statement about nine and a half or so years later. The amici raise the question of whether they're not so unreliable in those circumstances that we ought not to admit the statement, and your current suggestion is that we admit the statement for the purposes of 92 bis, but we allow cross-examination in order that they can be tested.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And let me add something, why we put them on our witness list at all. These are actually two witnesses who give the names of the victims that are in the schedules, and the victims are actually their relatives. The fact that they were killed in this incident is actually proven by them, and I don't think that we will rely on all the details, how the event happened, because they were so young, but their relatives were killed and that they were killed in the incident where they themselves also were present. I mean, this is -- this can be reliably -- can be led from them reliably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, you hear the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We don't really have anything further to add to what we put in our written motion. We've pointed out the problems here with the age of these two witnesses. The second one, as I recollect it, said "as best as I can remember now" is one of the phrases that he uses. I think that is 1231, the nine-year-old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose, just thinking aloud, Mr. Kay, about this, these were terrible events which people are unlikely to forget. However young they may have been at the time, it was bound to be impressed upon them in a way which perhaps in the normal course of events one would say, well, you're not going to recollect what happened ten years ago, but these sort of events ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That can always be said, but the difficulty is in actual comprehension at the time to have provided an accurate eyewitness account. One of the problems being of such tender years as 9 is that the picture can be coloured by subsequent events and family history to make the account of events very different from what it was before. It has to be recognised that the memories of children in relation to such events are probably not as good and reliable as those who are of older years, adults, who have more context in which to put events into, caused by human experience. And that goes for Witness 1201, the 11-year-old, as well. These are very, very young ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Anything you want to add in relation to these two?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question of reliability is a matter we have to consider in whether we should admit the statements, but here, given the events which these witnesses have described, which they are not likely to have forgotten, given their terrible nature, over the years, and given that their detail is a matter, the detail of the statements is a matter which can be tested by cross-examination, we think it right to admit the statements but subject to cross-examination of the witnesses. Yes. Yes. We can call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we start the next witness? Thank you. Your Honour, the witness will obviously be part heard. The question whether he should be part heard to Tuesday or Wednesday. Tuesday we have a fairly full-looking day, I think. Financial argument, human rights matter, and the general discussion about procedure. I'm entirely in your hands, and of course we want to use every available minute of time for evidence when we can, but he's been here once to go through the 92 bis process, and he's coming today and he'll go back and come again. It may be thought kind of him to say Wednesday morning first thing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see what his convenience is to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, while we're waiting for him -- I know he's in the distant room, a more distant room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we have some time, Mr. Blewitt will be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour sees the wonderful service you get. The podium is brought for you. The witness Helena Ranta is coming on the 10th -- the 12th. Very well. I'm not sure whether the 10th is being earmarked now for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a problem with the videolink on the 10th, I think, but it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly he's available on the 10th, but we'll keep telephoning him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the better understanding of those viewing, the witness made a statement on the 19th of January of the year 2001, which is in 46 paragraphs, originally without numbers but numbered for the purposes of this exercise. He's gone through the process of 92 bis with an official of the Tribunal in respect of that statement which he has corrected by a short additional statement of the 5th of February, 2003. And the Chamber has allowed that his evidence may be limited in this way that can, I suppose, be summarised in respect of all bar a limited number of paragraphs of the original statement which have been taken from him in the conventional way. There are a couple of exhibits to be produced as well, and with Your Honour's leave, I will simply run very quickly through the proofing summary, which is a summary of his evidence overall and runs to some 18 paragraphs, stopping at the appropriate places for exhibits and/or for live testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Paul Davies?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice just mentioned an additional statement dated the 5th of February. You announced this witness yesterday and I have all the material I received in connection with him and I have never received a statement dated the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that is an addendum which was referred to. Mr. Nice, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. It's part of the 92 bis package, as we've described them, and it can be found at the fifth page of that, although the page number is page 11, starting at the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you look at the documents you were given today, under the attestation, you will see the additional statement which is -- or addendum, rather, which is in the form of one or two changes. You will have a chance to read it before you cross-examine. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, are you an ITN reporter, having been an international reporter since 1983, you have extensive experience of the wars in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in Dubrovnik with your crew, or with first a larger crew and then a reduced crew between the 31st of October to the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence, summarised in the proofing summary, is that there were only a limited number of Croatian defenders of Dubrovnik, nightclub owners, waiters, tour guides, and so on, that the weapons of the Croats were in no way comparable to the JNA weapons which you describe as mighty, the JNA having completely surrounded the town from high ground of Zarkovica, Ivanica, having gunboats facing the town, using military planes to attack Srdj and the Cross next to it. You saw a mortar position in the city's woodland but that was a distance from the town, and we'll come to this maybe in a little more detail later. You observed a small number of heavy weapons, being no more than two pieces of mortars or small artillery at any given place and time. You observed that hundreds of shells were fired on Dubrovnik by the JNA for each shell that was fired by Croatian defenders. You were aware of one mobile artillery weapon on a flatbed truck used by Croatian defenders, and you thought that there was also a truck converted to transport personnel and supplies, probably both military and humanitarian, that was in use. And following your arrival in Dubrovnik, you noticed a large number of civilians who had fled villages taken over by the JNA, looking for safety in Dubrovnik old town, well known as a UNESCO world heritage site.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's all correct. In summary, a very one-sided affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By one-sided affair, you mean the fighting --

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: The fighting was extremely one-sided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we now see, please, the exhibit which is about, I think, a few minutes of an ITN report of this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Until now, the federal forces have concentrated their attack on areas outside the old city, but now their mortars are falling inside the ancient walls." "One exploded through the roof of a house built four centuries ago. In all, four mortars fell inside the city walls that day, shrapnel exploding into the convent. The tranquility of the 14th century Franciscan monastery, home of the Europe's oldest apothecary, was also shattered. As Friar Josef Sopta [phoen] tried to tell us about the damage to the monastery, his words were drowned by another attack." "Sad." "As the federal troops closed in, the few residents left on the streets took what cover they could. This woman had risked her life to rescue her dog from its kennel in the old harbour. "A day that started with prayer ended with pitched battles in the hilltops. Monday and the famous Stradun, Dubrovnik's main street, deserted in preparation for the inevitable resumption of this one-sided battle. "Residential areas devastated, with shells falling closer and closer to the old city, for the first time, striking its medieval walls. Down the centuries, Dubrovnik citizens have defied would be invaders. Now their old ramparts face 20th century war machines. But at least the walls offered some protection. Outside, there was no escape. "The Grand Hotel, probably Dubrovnik's finest, ablaze. But this was just a foretaste of the destruction that was to follow as the federal forces closed in. "Tuesday morning, and the attack everyone had feared but most secretly believed could never happen. A deliberate and sustained assault on the old city. This was not a case of shells going astray, it was a calculated decision to irreparably damage a city that is in its entirety a protected monument. Some shells appeared to bounce off the 100 foot high walls but others crashed into the city. The federal army was now using Soviet made wire-guided missiles against walls first built to keep out arrows and spears. "Missiles landing in the old port set boats and building ablaze. Among the witnesses to the attack was Britain's consul to Dubrovnik, Sarah Maraika [phoen], whose husband is Croatian." "I never thought that the old city would be damaged. It's the same way that one thinks of Venice or Paris or Canterbury. I think it was thought that the old city was inviolable and it's been proven that that isn't either. This was built as a siege town." "That's five shells. Five shells as we've been talking." "As we've been talking, and that's quite minimal, isn't it, compared to what we've gone through earlier today." "From the terrace of the Hotel Argentina, the European Community observers also watched the destruction, powerless to intervene." "They're shooting for the tower in the old city. They just missed it." "But they were forced to run for shelter when mortars fell around their hotel. "The observers spent hours pinned down by mortars exploding outside. Plans to evacuate their team by sea had to be postponed because of the raging battle. "In the hotel bar, scenes reminiscent of London's east end during the blitz. Locals singing traditional songs to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough now. Just remind us, if you would, of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 10th to the 14th of November, I think, for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Davies?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we move on to the testimony I'll take from you in the conventional way, may the witness produce two maps that will be, I hope, of use. One to become Exhibit 326, tab 24. It shows the larger area and has hotels identified on it by the witness. And we can see there, for those not familiar with the area of Dubrovnik, the old town just above the word "Hotel" of Grand Hotel Imperial, and then the harbour up -- or the Luka harbour, Gruz, up on the left there. The old harbour of the town, Mr. Davies, where we can really see it here, is to the right of the old town, to the left of the letter H of Hotel Excelsior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then although it doesn't show it on this map, the river, the Rijeka, is on the left of the plan, running up in a north-easterly direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is tab 23, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 24. 326, tab 24, I think, with leave of the Court. This one is marked, of course. I'm not sure, as the only one is -- maybe Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judging by the index we've been given, that is right. 23 and 24, they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 23 and 24, in which case I stand corrected and apologise for that. May we put the other map on the overhead projector, then, tab 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This shows clearly the harbour to the right which we saw in that footage, and we see the walled town or city. The road, or the route that you were describing or showing indeed on your film, empty of people walking it, is that the large street running left to right towards the top of the plan?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's correct. The Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not called Stradun here, is it? All we've got is the word Platca here. Is that it, though?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll now go to what is the 32nd paragraph in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, we ought to get the exhibits into order. The 92 bis statement and addendum should be the next exhibit number, and then the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 394 for the statement, Your Honour. The video is Prosecutor's Exhibit 395.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, you actually stayed on longer than all other non-residents, I think, and were there on your own for a time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: With a cameraman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With one cameraman.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After everybody else had left. Help us, please, with your experience generally of the shelling; how it was targeted, where it appeared to be targeted, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was -- there was a mixture, really. The majority of it didn't seem to have an obvious target, certainly not to us. After a period of shelling, sometimes during a period of shelling, we would attempt to get close to what was being targeted, and quite often this was just housing, no specific military purpose that we could see. And also during that time, we would be watching very closely for any signs of outgoing fire, any reason that might attract the shelling, and very often there simply was none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The road, the main road for Dubrovnik, which we can see on the larger map, did that appear to be targeted at all?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was targeted, yes, and also the housing that's very close to it was targeted over a period of some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with the larger map, if the usher would be good -- not the larger map, the map showing the larger area, tab 23. The island of Lokrum is seen to the right of the map. What was the position about Lokrum? Who possessed it? Was it being shelled?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It was still possessed by the Croatians, and it was a regular target to the extent that I believe it's a national park, or large areas of it are. So, wooded. And it was often on fire. The hotel where we were based and where the monitors were based, the Hotel Argentina, is directly opposite the island of Lokrum and there were many nights when the fires on the island continued through the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Attacks on residential areas, how severe? Were houses just damaged or were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Damaged. Mostly damaged. It wasn't a case of streets being levelled or that type of damage, but severe damage. I mean, damage, shells dropping through floors and causing extreme damage to the individual buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with tab 23 which shows, of course, the old town to which we may turn in detail later, but also the wider urban area of Dubrovnik, can you point to any areas you can recall now having visited when there had been targeting or apparent targeting of residential areas? You can see it on the overhead projector, and you will be given a pointer if necessary.

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: Yes. All right. The area leading to the port seemed to take a lot of incoming shells. It was difficult to understand, because that was only housing. The areas around the coast were targeted, and we visited them during the time that they were being targeted. There's a very large hotel here called the Libertas. We went there, I believe, one night as there was shelling, and it was on fire and there were many refugees in the cellars of the building, taking what shelter they could. Other areas that we saw targeted regularly were the -- these hotels here along this stretch by the Hotel Argentina. This hotel here, the Hotel Belvedere, was very, very badly damaged, set on fire and caused a great deal of damage to that. This hotel, the Excelsior, was also very, very badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The plan doesn't have a scale. Maybe I can find one for next week when I'm afraid you will have to return, but give us an idea, how long does it take to drive from the old town - let's use that as a focal point - to something like Hotel Libertas if the roads are uncrowded?

utterances.speaker: PAUL DAVIES
utterances.text: It would take ten minutes. Not much more than ten minutes. And the roads during this period of time were deserted. So it was quite easy and there was no particular reason to comply with one-way regulations or anything, so it would take ten minutes at the most to get from the old town to, say, Hotel Libertas. Ten, 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've come to the time to adjourn, Mr. Nice. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Convenient moment for me. The return date for the witness may be a matter which should reflect his convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Davies, I'm sorry you've been inconvenienced by having to come here twice already. We can't finish your evidence today, so we must ask you to come back next week. We're not sitting on Monday. On Tuesday we have some administrative things to deal with, so we could deal with your evidence on Wednesday, but if it was more convenient, we could find time on Tuesday to deal with it. I don't know if you have any particular views on that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tuesday would be easier, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we should try and accommodate that. We have a discussion about witnesses first, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one matter that involves other parties coming especially and obviously that must be taken care of on Tuesday. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a discrete argument about the financial report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That can go into Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That can go into Wednesday, as can the discussion about procedure matters that I must, on this occasion, cover in some detail because I want to bring you absolutely up-to-date with where we are in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if we can hear the matter involving the other parties Tuesday in the first session and continue with the witness after the first break, which would be half past ten --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will probably allow him to make a Tuesday morning flight, if he wants to, that would get him here in time for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's convenient to you, Mr. Davies, could we ask you to be back on Tuesday at half past ten, and we will hear your evidence then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I must formally tell you not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. But if you want to talk to them about your arrangements or anything of that sort, of course you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 9.00 Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
